checks.claim: Key: the number of atoms of each element is always the same after a reaction (atoms are rearranged, never made or destroyed)
checks.note: Grokipedia: atoms are 'neither created nor destroyed, only rearranged among the molecules'; total mass of reactants equals products.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'the number of molecules' is not always the same
checks.note: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2: two molecules become three. Some reactions keep the count, but the stem asks what is ALWAYS the same, so the choice is wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'the way the atoms are joined together' changes
checks.note: A reaction is the breaking and forming of bonds between atoms.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'the space the substances take up' can change (a gas given off)
checks.note: CaCO3 + 2HCl gives CO2 gas, effervescence.

checks.claim: Context: bonds break and form, atoms regroup, no atom made or destroyed, so mass stays the same; marble fizzing in acid gives off a gas
Stem: Boyle sealed tin in glass, heated it for hours, broke the seal and weighed the metal, which had grown heavier
checks.note: Boyle 1673, New Experiments to make Fire and Flame Ponderable (annexed to Essays of Effluviums), Exp. V: 2 oz of tin filings in a small retort sealed at the apex, 'kept in the fire above two hours', broken at the apex, the tin weighed 'two Ounces twelve Grains'. Exp. IV used a bolt-head (a long-necked flask); metal and calx weighed without the glass. 'Glass flask' is a fair plain word for his retort.

checks.claim: Stem: Boyle decided particles of fire had passed in through the glass
checks.note: Boyle, Corollary III: 'Igneous particles were trajected through the Glass'. Science History Institute: 'fiery particles that were able to pass through the walls of glass vessels'.

checks.claim: Stem: Lavoisier in 1774 heated tin sealed in glass with air and weighed the whole sealed vessel before and after heating, before opening it
checks.note: Wikipedia: in spring 1774 he calcined tin and lead in sealed vessels. Memoir 'on the calcination of tin in closed vessels', Memoires de l'Academie for 1774 (published 1777), 8 onces of tin, whole apparatus weighed at various points (web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/classicalcs/lavoisier.html). Grokipedia's Lavoisier page dates his sealed-vessel work to 1772, but the tin memoir and Wikipedia give 1774; 1774 stands.

checks.claim: Key: the balance showed no change
checks.note: Grokipedia: in 1774 he heated tin and lead in closed containers and 'the total mass of the vessel and contents remained unchanged'. SBU teaching page: 'total weight of the sealed retort is unchanged'; 'when opened, air rushes in and total weight increases'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: a gain from fire through the glass; a gain from the heavy crust; a loss from tin burning into smoke
checks.note: The calx forms, but the sealed total does not change, so no gain or loss is right.

checks.claim: Context: the tin gained 3.12 grains and the air shut in with it lost 3.12 grains
checks.note: Giunta's worked exercise on Lavoisier's 1774 data: 8 onces of tin, 15 1/3 grains of air; solids 3.12 grains heavier, gas 3.12 grains lighter.

checks.claim: Context: 'Boyle's tin had really grown heavier, but from the air inside his flask, not from fire'
checks.note: That the gain came from air, not fire, is right. 'Inside his flask' is doubtful: Boyle's 2 oz of tin gained 12 grains, four times Lavoisier's 3.12 grains from 8 onces, in a small retort sealed hot with thin air; a history article judges his experiment faulty, 'presumably the seal was not tight'. Fix: 'Boyle's tin had really grown heavier, but from air, not from fire.'

checks.claim: Context: 'He even heard outside air rush in when he broke the seal, to fill the place of the air the tin had taken up'
checks.note: Boyle drove the fumes out and sealed the retort hot, and he gives the reason himself: the air rushed in 'because when the Retort was sealed the Air within it was highly rarified'. The thin air left by sealing it hot was the main cause; the air taken up by the tin was at most a small part. Fix: 'He even heard outside air rush in when he broke the seal, which he put down to having sealed the flask while it was hot.' (Or cut the sentence.)

checks.claim: Stem: Stahl's phlogiston theory guided chemists across Europe for most of the 1700s
checks.note: Becher's terra pinguis (1660s) renamed phlogiston by Stahl by 1703; influential 'across Germany, France, and Britain for over a century', until Lavoisier in the 1770s-1780s.

checks.claim: Stem: burning releases phlogiston, leaving ash or, from a metal, a calx
checks.note: Phlogiston 'escapes into the surrounding air, leaving behind a residue known as calx or ash'.

checks.claim: Key: a calx weighing more than its metal was the hardest observation for the theory
checks.note: Metals should have lost phlogiston, yet they weighed more as calx; Grokipedia names the weight gain on calcination as the theory's anomaly.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a flame in a closed jar going out was explained by the theory
checks.note: Air became saturated with phlogiston, so 'flames extinguish in confined spaces'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a burnt log leaving little ash was explained by the theory
checks.note: The weight loss of wood turning to ash was counted as support.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: charcoal turning a calx back into metal was explained by the theory
checks.note: Charcoal 'was seen as a phlogiston source' that restored the metal.

checks.claim: Context: defenders gave phlogiston strange powers, even a weight below zero
checks.note: Chardenon (1764) proposed levity or negative weight; Guyton de Morveau (1772) anti-gravitational properties (Grokipedia). Encyclopedia.com: the gain 'was usually explained away by the theory that phlogiston had negative weight'.

checks.claim: Context: wood gave off most of itself as phlogiston; air in a closed jar took phlogiston until it could take no more; charcoal gave phlogiston back to a calx
checks.note: A fair plain-words account of how the theory read these observations.

checks.claim: Context: Lavoisier's sealed-vessel weighings showed the calx's extra weight came from the air
checks.note: The tin and lead sealed-vessel experiments 'conclusively confirmed that the increase in weight of metals on calcination was due to combination with air'.

checks.claim: Stem: marble is a rock made of calcium carbonate; it fizzes in dilute hydrochloric acid
checks.note: Calcite 'forms the bulk of limestone, chalk, marble'; the acid reaction 'produces effervescence due to the rapid evolution of CO2 bubbles'. (Some marble is dolomitic; the plain statement is a fair grade-level simplification.)

checks.claim: Key: the reading falls because a gas made escapes into the air
checks.note: In an open container 'the carbon dioxide gas escapes into the atmosphere, causing the mass of the system to decrease'. RSC: in open systems gases 'give the false impression that mass has been lost'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: some of the marble's atoms are used up
checks.note: No atom is destroyed in a reaction.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: some of the mass is turned into energy
checks.note: The mass change from chemical energy is far too small to measure (Planck, via Wikipedia; Grokipedia: energy-mass conversions in ordinary chemistry are negligible). It is not why the reading falls.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the gas has no weight at all
checks.note: A named misconception: 'some students think that gases have no mass'.

checks.claim: Context: CaCO3 + acid gives calcium chloride, water and CO2; in a sealed flask the reading stays unchanged
checks.note: Equation CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2 (Grokipedia); closing the system shows the mass constant (RSC).

checks.claim: Stem: magnesium burns with a brilliant white light and gives a white powder
checks.note: RSC: 'Magnesium burns with a bright white light'; complete product is white. Grokipedia Magnesium: 'brilliant white flame'.

checks.claim: Stem numbers: 0.24 g magnesium gives 0.40 g of powder, 0.16 g extra
checks.note: Checked by molar mass: 0.24 g Mg x 40.30/24.31 = 0.398 g MgO, so 0.16 g of oxygen. The numbers are the ideal 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO result.

checks.claim: Key: the extra mass is oxygen that joined it from the air
checks.note: RSC: the increase in mass 'corresponds to the mass of oxygen'. (In a real crucible a little magnesium nitride also forms; the stem's numbers fit pure MgO, so the key stands at grade level.)

checks.claim: Wrong choices: heat soaked up; gas from the burner clung to it; new matter made
checks.note: Heat adds no measurable mass; no matter is created; the gain is oxygen from the air.

checks.claim: Context: the lid is lifted only a little now and then, to let air in without letting the powder escape
checks.note: RSC: lift the lid 'a little to allow some oxygen to get in'; if lifted too long 'the magnesium oxide product will begin to escape'.

checks.claim: Key: most of the log's mass goes into the air as invisible gases
checks.note: Wood's carbon and hydrogen are 'completely converted to carbon dioxide (CO2) and water vapour (H2O)', both invisible.

checks.claim: Context: wood is mostly carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
checks.note: 'roughly 50% carbon by weight, 40% oxygen and 5% hydrogen'.

checks.claim: Context and stem: only the minerals, a few percent, stay behind as ash; a tiny share of the mass
checks.note: 'dry wood ... typically yields 1-3% ash by dry weight', mostly calcium and potassium compounds; hardwoods such as oak at the higher end.

checks.claim: Context: the gases and ash together weigh more than the log, because of the oxygen that joined it
checks.note: Checked: 1 kg of dry wood holds about 0.5 kg of carbon, which becomes about 1.8 kg of CO2, plus about 0.45 kg of water vapour from its hydrogen; the products far outweigh the log.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: into nothing; into heat and light; into the ground
checks.note: Matter is not destroyed; the mass carried by heat and light is too small to measure; the mass rises as gas, not into the ground.

checks.claim: Key: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2 says hydrogen peroxide breaks into water and oxygen
checks.note: Decomposition 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: water and oxygen join to make it (reversed); it is a mixture of water and oxygen; it reacts with water
checks.note: Reactants on the left, products on the right; H2O2 'is a chemical compound' (Grokipedia), not a mixture; water is a product, not a reactant.

checks.claim: Context: the arrow is read as yields
checks.note: OpenStax: reactants 'react to yield' products.

checks.claim: Context: hydrogen peroxide foams on blood because catalase speeds the reaction; the bubbles are oxygen
checks.note: Grokipedia Hydrogen peroxide: effervescence on wounds, 'catalyzed by catalase enzymes present in blood'; catalase gives 'water and molecular oxygen'.

checks.claim: Stem: iron oxide (Fe2O3) is the stuff of hematite and, with water bound in, of rust
checks.note: Fe2O3 'serves as the primary constituent of the mineral hematite'; rust is a hydrated variant, 4Fe + 3O2 + 2xH2O -> 2Fe2O3.xH2O.

checks.claim: Key: the 3 in front of O2 means three molecules of oxygen take part
checks.note: Coefficients 'represent the relative number of molecules, formula units, or moles'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: three atoms (it is six); each molecule holds three atoms (that is ozone, O3); three grams
checks.note: 3O2 = 3 x 2 = 6 atoms; ozone is O3, 'three oxygen atoms bonded together'; coefficients count particles, not grams.

checks.claim: Context: 2Fe2O3 holds six oxygen atoms; a number in front counts whole molecules
checks.note: 2 x 3 = 6. Strictly, Fe2O3 is counted in formula units, not molecules, but the context never calls it a molecule, and 'molecules' is the NGSS grade-8 word.

checks.claim: Stem: a Bunsen burner's blue flame is methane burning in air
checks.note: The burner uses 'natural gas or propane'; natural gas is 'primarily methane'; the blue flame signifies complete combustion. True of the usual mains-gas burner. Optional softening: 'A Bunsen burner fed with natural gas burns methane in air'.

checks.claim: Key: the right side of CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O holds four oxygen atoms
checks.note: CO2 gives 1 x 2 = 2, 2H2O gives 2 x 1 = 2, total 4. Left: 2O2 = 4. Carbon 1 = 1, hydrogen 4 = 2 x 2 = 4.

checks.claim: Wrong choices Two, Three, Six are wrong counts
checks.note: Only four is correct.

checks.claim: Context: two oxygen molecules on the left hold four; one carbon and four hydrogen on both sides
Stem: lead nitrate and potassium iodide solutions are both colourless and make a bright yellow solid at once
checks.note: Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 + 2KNO3, 'a bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide'; two colourless solutions, the precipitate forms instantly (MIT and UW chemistry demonstration pages).

checks.claim: Key: the balance shows the same mass
checks.note: RSC recommends this precipitation reaction for showing conservation of mass because no gas is made or used.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: a solid weighs more than a liquid; a new substance added; the solutions used up
checks.note: Named misconceptions: solids thought to 'weigh more than their liquid form', matter 'used up'. Nothing enters from outside.

checks.claim: Context: potassium nitrate stays dissolved; no atom comes in or goes out
checks.note: Potassium and nitrate ions stay in solution; only lead iodide precipitates.

unit_notes: 9 ok, 1 error, 0 uncertain. The one error is in 440332c57b's context: Boyle himself put the rush of air on opening down to the retort having been sealed hot ('the Air within it was highly rarified'), not to air taken up by the tin; the same context's 'from the air inside his flask' is also doubtful (his gain was too large for a small, hot-sealed retort), so say 'from air, not from fire'. Grokipedia dates Lavoisier's sealed-vessel work to 1772, but his tin memoir and Wikipedia give spring 1774, so the stem's 1774 stands. Primary Boyle text read at distantreader.org (EarlyPrint transcription of the 1673 Essays of Effluviums with the annexed New Experiments).
